newsitem.title: BRAZIL: MOTOR RACING-KEN STILL ENJOYS LIFE IN THE FAST LANE.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-KEN STILL ENJOYS LIFE IN THE FAST LANE.

text.p: - Ken Tyrrell, the most venerable figure in a Grand Prix pitlane, is more of an inspiration than an institution in Formula One.
He represents a way of life that most of his rivals have forgotten but envy. At 72, he is racing for fun -- and still enjoying it.
"Of course, it is my business," he conceded. "But that is not all there is to it. I actually enjoy the travel, the places we go to and the races.
"You don't think I'd have gone on so long if I didn't, do you?"
When he laughs, it is in huge guffaws that fill the room and draw a crowd. In Brazil the fans are in awe of him.
But everything about Ken Tyrrell is big. He is tall, has a hawk-like bearing and a towering physical presence.
He is also the only man who can claim to have taught Jackie Stewart a thing or two about Grand Prix racing.
"We had a fantastic relationship when he was a driver and we still do now that he is a rival team owner," said Tyrrell.
"But that is the way it should be. I know everything has become a lot more professional and competitive but we are still normal people below the surface, aren't we?

"I like to enjoy the racing and I think that is the way it should be. But that does not mean I don't want to be successful. It just happens that it is very difficult to win races -- far more difficult than it has ever been before."

It may be 24 years since a Tyrrell driver won the world drivers' championship and 14 since one of his cars won a race. But that does not bother him or put him off what most men of his age would avoid -- a year-long schedule of tough travel, time changes, long hours and constant political hassle.

This week he has had to face another of many behind-the-scenes disputes over the new 1997 Concorde Agreement, a document which he, Frank Williams and Ron Dennis declined to sign last year in protest at what they believed to be less than fair terms offered.

Tyrrell, above all, is a survivor. While several of the big-name teams who were his rivals in the 1970s and 1980s have disappeared -- normally because of financial problems -- he has carried on racing.

The famous names have included Lotus and Brabham, both also world champion outfits, and the recent demise of Lola -- after only one Grand Prix at which they failed to qualify for the race -- serves only to rub in the point.
Tyrrell, like many other successful businessmen, knows how to balance his books and keep on trading when others fall by the wayside.

He is not afraid of change or delegation. For the last six years, he has been nominally chairman of the Tyrrell Racing Organisation while his son Bob Tyrrell and the engineer, Harvey Postlethwaite, share the duties of being split managing directors for the commerical and technical halves of the company.

"I soon learned about making decisions, early in my life," said Tyrrell. "I realised when I was a saloon car driver that I would be better off on the management side of things -- and that is how it all began."
One of the most famous of many Tyrrell tales is the one that he recites when asked how he became interested in motor racing.
As a member of a village football team he went on an organised outing to Silverstone, sank a few beers on the coach and had a fantastic day out.
"I was hooked and that was it," he said.
But he has not lost his love for soccer and remains a supporter of his favourite team, Tottenham.

When Spurs reached the F.A. Cup final in 1987 the match clashed with a Grand Prix weekend in Europe. "I flew back and forth so I could be at Wembley and I got back in time for the race, too," said Tyrrell.
Never one to shy from risking his cars with young drivers, Tyrrell can claim to have unearthed and given debuts to many future big names, including Stewart and, in more recent times, Jean Alesi.
"I like seeing new guys come in and do well but that is not the reason this has happened. That would be too romantic," he admitted.
"No, the truth is that I have usually needed to switch to a different driver for other reasons -- normally business reasons. That is one of the ways we have managed to keep on going all these years."
